He sells Locke on because the boy's ambitions have already cost lives and threaten to draw exactly the kind of attention a gang of child thieves cannot survive.
characters.name: The Thiefmaker

characters.description: Capa Barsavi's only daughter and, since her brothers are blunter instruments, the most capable of his children. She has known Locke since they were both children in the same gang and treats him with rough affection. Her father intends her to inherit his position, and has settled views about whom she ought to marry in order to hold it.
characters.name: Nazca Barsavi

characters.description: Twin sisters who serve as Capa Barsavi's personal bodyguards and are the most celebrated shark-fighters in Camorr, drawing crowds at the floating carnival where they kill in the water for the city's entertainment. Silent, identical and universally feared, they wear trophies taken from their kills.
characters.name: Cheryn and Raiza Berangias

characters.description: A figure nobody has seen clearly who has begun killing Capa Barsavi's gang leaders one at a time, leaving no witnesses and no explanation. He appears to want the capa's chair, and to command resources no Camorri criminal should be able to afford. Barsavi's people cannot find him, and the killings are steadily emptying the capa's court while the city's thieves take sides in advance.
characters.name: The Grey King

characters.description: A Bondsmage of Karthain, one of the mercenary sorcerers whose guild is feared across the continent and priced accordingly. He is accompanied everywhere by a scorpion hawk called Vestris, through whose eyes he can see. The Bondsmagi are protected by one rule that everybody obeys: harm a single member and the entire guild answers, so no one in Camorr will lift a hand against him whatever he does while under contract.
characters.name: The Falconer

characters.description: A Gentleman Bastard raised with Locke, Jean and the Sanzas under Father Chains, and the only girl among them. By Locke's account she is better than he is at every part of the work. She has not been in Camorr for years, and Locke, who has loved her since they were children, is unable to discuss her sensibly with anyone.
characters.name: Sabetha Belacoros

characters.description: The elderly Countess Amberglass, long widowed and childless, who presides over the noblewomen's gatherings in her glass tower and spends most of them apparently dozing over her knitting while her guests talk around her. Camorri society treats her as a harmless fixture and speaks freely in front of her.
characters.name: Dona Angiavesta Vorchenza

recaps.ending: Locke kills Capa Raza aboard the Floating Grave and survives the fight only just, with Jean carrying him out. Raza's revenge on Barsavi is complete but his second scheme fails: the attack he prepared for Camorr's assembled nobility at the duke's feast is stopped because Locke gave the warning to the Spider in time. That officer turns out to be Dona Vorchenza, the elderly countess nobody took seriously. She knows exactly who Locke is and cannot prove any of it, and she lets him go rather than pursue him. The Falconer is collected by his own guild, mutilated and out of his mind; the Bondsmagi make it plain that what was done to him will be answered in their own time and on their own schedule, so Locke and Jean leave Camorr with an enemy that outlasts the city. Calo, Galdo, Bug and Nazca Barsavi are dead, the Gentlemen Bastards' hoarded fortune is scattered, and the temple that hid them is finished as a home. Locke and Jean take ship out of Camorr as the last two of the crew Chains raised, with their skills, each other, and very little else.
recaps.in_short: In the canal city of Camorr, thieves live under the Secret Peace: they may rob the common folk as they please and must never touch the nobility. Locke Lamora, raised by a fraudulent blind priest to be a confidence artist rather than a cutpurse, breaks that rule for a living, running elaborate swindles on the aristocracy with his small crew, the Gentlemen Bastards. While he works his latest mark, a masked figure called the Grey King begins murdering the crime lord Capa Barsavi's captains, and a hired sorcerer of the Bondsmagi forces Locke to serve the Grey King's scheme. The trap closes: Barsavi is destroyed, the Grey King takes the city's underworld as Capa Raza, and three of the Gentlemen Bastards are murdered along with the crew's fortune. Locke and Jean Tannen, the only survivors, take the sorcerer apart, expose Raza's plan to slaughter Camorr's nobility to the duke's secret intelligence chief, and Locke kills Raza himself. They leave the city avenged, ruined, and permanently marked by the sorcerers' guild.

recaps.text: Camorr is a canal city built on the indestructible glass ruins of a vanished people, ruled by a duke and his nobility above and by Capa Vencarlo Barsavi's gangs below. The two halves are joined by the Secret Peace: the underworld may rob the common folk freely so long as it never touches an aristocrat, and the watch leaves it alone in return. Locke Lamora, sold as a child to the fraudulent blind priest Father Chains and raised in the vault beneath his temple, now leads the Gentlemen Bastards - Jean Tannen, the twins Calo and Galdo Sanza, and the boy Bug. To Barsavi they are a small gang of unambitious thieves paying their tribute. In fact they break the Secret Peace as a profession, running long confidence games on the nobility and hoarding the proceeds unspent in a vault under the temple. Their current mark is Don Lorenzo Salvara, whom Locke, disguised as a northern brandy merchant, persuades to invest heavily in a venture that does not exist, and whose sharper wife Sofia has to be handled as carefully as the don himself. Interleaved chapters show the crew's childhood and Chains teaching them the trade.

Barsavi's court is in trouble. Someone calling himself the Grey King has begun murdering the capa's gang leaders one at a time, without witnesses, and Barsavi has withdrawn to his moored galleon refusing to move against an enemy he cannot find. Summoned by the capa's daughter Nazca, an old friend of Locke's from their orphanage days, Locke learns that Barsavi means her to inherit and means Locke to marry her in order to steady the succession. The Salvara game continues to pay well. Then the Grey King reaches for Locke directly: he is taken by a Bondsmage of Karthain called the Falconer, a hired sorcerer whose guild nobody dares harm, and delivered to the Grey King, who orders Locke to impersonate him at a parley with Barsavi. Refusal is not on offer: the Bondsmage's presence removes every option that involves force, and the errand will put Locke in a room between the two most dangerous men in Camorr.

The Grey King's grip tightens. Nazca Barsavi, going to negotiate on her father's behalf, is murdered and her body returned to the capa, which removes any prospect of a settlement. Locke keeps the Salvara game running while preparing to stand in front of Barsavi wearing another man's name, and Jean, the only person who knows the whole shape of it, can find no way out. At the Echo Hole, Locke goes through with the impersonation and Barsavi springs the ambush he has spent days preparing. It is Barsavi who has been played. His own bodyguards, the Berangias sisters, turn on him, his sons are killed, and the Grey King reveals himself and has the capa drowned in the same cask his daughter's body came back in. The Grey King takes Camorr's underworld for himself under the name Capa Raza. Locke is stabbed, sealed in a barrel and thrown into the bay. Jean pulls him out alive. They return to the temple and find Calo, Galdo and Bug murdered in the vault below it and the crew's entire fortune gone.

Locke, badly wounded and half destroyed by grief, is kept alive largely by Jean's stubbornness while Camorr's gangs swear to their new capa. Raza consolidates fast, buying loyalty with the money he took from the Gentlemen Bastards and dispensing favours from Barsavi's old galleon, and the city adjusts to him within days. Locke refuses to leave while the man is alive, which reduces the two of them to a plan with no crew, no money and no protection behind it. At the same time the other danger the Salvara con has stirred up comes closer: the duke's secret intelligence service, run by an officer known only as the Spider, has been hunting the thief the nobility call the Thorn of Camorr, and the trail of the brandy swindle leads to him. Locke begins improvising a way to reach a man guarded by an entire underworld and by a Bondsmage.

Locke and Jean go after Raza with the only tools they have left. Locke works his way back into the city's business under a string of borrowed identities while Jean deals with the more direct obstacles: confronting the Berangias sisters, he kills them both. The pair then take the Falconer, whose protection proves less absolute than he believed. They kill his scorpion hawk, which unhinges him, and then cut out his tongue and take his fingers so that he can never work sorcery again, leaving his guild a living man to collect and a message they will not forget. Raza's motive is now clear: he is the surviving son of a merchant family destroyed years earlier by Barsavi with the duke's tacit consent, the Berangias sisters were his sisters, and every killing since has been payment against that debt. It is equally clear that he does not intend to stop with Barsavi, and that Camorr's nobility are the rest of the account.

Raza's remaining plan is aimed at the aristocracy, who will all be gathered in one place for the duke's feast in the sky-tower of Raven's Reach. Locke, caught by the duke's secret service before he can move, discovers that the Spider is Dona Vorchenza, the elderly countess the whole city has been dismissing for decades. He trades what he knows for the freedom to act; the warning reaches her in time and the nobility survive the attack Raza had prepared for them. Locke then goes after Raza in person. Aboard the Floating Grave he kills him, at very nearly the cost of his own life, and Jean gets him out. Calo, Galdo, Bug and Nazca are avenged, the crew's hoarded fortune is scattered beyond recovery, and Locke and Jean are the only two left of the family Chains built.

characters.description: A spirited young man left responsible for his mother and sister after his father's death. Proud, generous, and quick to act against cruelty, he goes to London seeking help from his wealthy uncle Ralph and accepts work far from home.
characters.name: Nicholas Nickleby

characters.description: Nicholas's beautiful younger sister, newly reduced from a comfortable rural life to dependence on her uncle. Gentle but perceptive, she tries to support her mother and bears the family's reversals with more steadiness than her sheltered upbringing might suggest.
characters.name: Kate Nickleby

characters.description: The widowed mother of Nicholas and Kate. Affectionate, talkative, and easily distracted by hopeful fantasies, she depends on her children while remaining convinced that favorable turns are always close at hand.
characters.name: Mrs Nickleby

characters.description: The wealthy uncle to whom the bereaved Nicklebys appeal for aid. A cold and calculating moneylender, he views dependence as weakness and offers assistance chiefly when it can serve his interests or assert his authority.
characters.name: Ralph Nickleby

characters.description: Ralph Nickleby's eccentric clerk, outwardly marked by shabby clothes, broken speech, and abrupt behavior. His strange manner conceals sympathy for Nicholas and Kate, and he quietly tries to shield them from their uncle's designs.
characters.name: Newman Noggs

characters.description: The brutal proprietor of Dotheboys Hall in Yorkshire, a school where unwanted boys are neglected and exploited for profit. He recruits Nicholas as an assistant master by presenting the institution far more favorably than it deserves.
characters.name: Wackford Squeers

characters.description: A frail, frightened older pupil at Dotheboys Hall who has no known family and is treated as the school's servant and chief target. Despite years of deprivation, he responds to Nicholas's first kindness with immediate loyalty.
characters.name: Smike

characters.description: A forthright young Yorkshire farmer who visits the Squeers family and quickly takes to Nicholas. His plain speech, humor, and instinctive fairness make him an important friendly presence near Dotheboys Hall.
characters.name: John Browdie

characters.description: A flamboyant actor-manager who leads a provincial theatrical company with his wife and children. He meets Nicholas on the road, recognizes his potential usefulness onstage, and welcomes both Nicholas and Smike into the troupe.
characters.name: Vincent Crummles

characters.description: One of two benevolent twin merchants who encounter Nicholas after his return to London. Frank and warm in manner, the brothers conduct business as a form of stewardship and offer the young man employment without demanding that he surrender his independence.
characters.name: Charles Cheeryble

characters.description: Charles Cheeryble's equally generous twin and business partner. He shares his brother's delight in relieving hardship and judges Nicholas by his conduct rather than by his poverty.
characters.name: Ned Cheeryble

characters.description: The Cheeryble brothers' good-natured nephew, recently returned from abroad. He becomes part of the welcoming circle that offers the Nickleby family friendship and stability after their harsh dependence on Ralph.
characters.name: Frank Cheeryble

characters.description: A young woman caring for her indebted, invalid father in conditions of genteel poverty. Her patience and quiet dignity impress Nicholas when the Cheerybles ask him to assist the family without wounding their pride.
characters.name: Madeline Bray

characters.description: An elderly, grasping moneylender who has gained power over Arthur Bray's debts. He presents his proposed marriage to Madeline as the price of rescuing her father, treating her vulnerability as a commercial opportunity.
characters.name: Arthur Gride

recaps.ending: Newman Noggs and Brooker expose Ralph Nickleby's crimes and reveal that Smike was Ralph's lost son. Ralph realizes that his persecution of Nicholas helped drive his own child through suffering and death, and he kills himself. Arthur Gride's scheme is defeated when the documents proving Madeline's inheritance are recovered; Madeline is free and eventually marries Nicholas. Frank Cheeryble marries Kate, while the brothers' generosity gives both couples security. Wackford Squeers is transported after his criminal dealings are uncovered, and the neglected pupils rebel against Dotheboys Hall and scatter home. Nicholas and Kate return with their spouses to the Nickleby family's old country home, accompanied by Mrs Nickleby and the loyal Newman Noggs. Nicholas and Madeline have children and preserve Smike's memory. The Cheerybles continue as friends and benefactors, and the surviving family gains the affectionate, stable household that Ralph's greed repeatedly tried to deny them.
recaps.in_short: After his father's death, Nicholas Nickleby seeks help from his rich uncle Ralph, who sends him to teach at the abusive Dotheboys Hall and places his sister Kate in poorly paid work. Nicholas attacks the school's proprietor Squeers for beating the vulnerable pupil Smike, escapes with the boy, and briefly joins the Crummles theatrical company. Returning to London, he protects Kate from Ralph's predatory associates and finds honorable employment with the generous Cheeryble brothers. Nicholas falls in love with Madeline Bray, whom Ralph tries to force into marriage with the old moneylender Arthur Gride. The plan collapses when her father dies and evidence of her inheritance is recovered. Squeers and Ralph also try to seize Smike, whose health fails after years of abuse. After Smike dies, Ralph learns that the boy was his own son and kills himself. Squeers is transported, Dotheboys Hall breaks apart, Nicholas marries Madeline, Kate marries Frank Cheeryble, and the family returns to a secure country home with Newman Noggs.

recaps.text: Nicholas Nickleby's father dies after losing the family's savings, leaving Nicholas, his sister Kate, and their mother with little support. They travel to London and appeal to the dead man's wealthy brother Ralph. Ralph regards the family as a burden but arranges work that keeps them under his control: Kate is placed with a milliner, while Nicholas is sent north as assistant to Wackford Squeers at Dotheboys Hall. Ralph's damaged clerk Newman Noggs privately warns Nicholas that Squeers is dangerous. At the school Nicholas discovers hungry, sick, and unwanted boys being systematically neglected. Squeers and his family use the pupils as cheap labor and direct special cruelty toward Smike, a frail youth with no known relatives. Nicholas tries to protect him while learning how thoroughly the school depends on fear.

Smike runs away but is captured and brought back to Dotheboys Hall. When Squeers beats him, Nicholas can no longer remain an observer: he turns the beating on Squeers, renounces his post, and leaves the school. Smike follows and begs to stay with him, and Nicholas accepts responsibility for his vulnerable companion. In London, Kate's position deteriorates. She is transferred from exhausting millinery work to employment that exposes her to Ralph's fashionable associates, including Sir Mulberry Hawk, whose attention is insulting and threatening. Ralph treats Kate's distress as insignificant because preserving his business relationships matters more to him. Newman Noggs becomes the siblings' covert ally, passing warnings and watching for ways to defeat his employer's schemes.

On the road, Nicholas and Smike meet actor-manager Vincent Crummles and join his theatrical company. Nicholas adapts plays and performs successfully, while Smike is given safety and a place among people who accept him. News from Newman brings Nicholas back to London, where he learns how Ralph's associates have treated Kate. Nicholas confronts Hawk and later pursues him after another provocation, ending the immediate threat to his sister but deepening Ralph's hatred. Nicholas then meets the benevolent merchants Charles and Ned Cheeryble. Impressed by his courage and honesty, they give him a secure post and extend practical kindness to the whole family. Their help allows Nicholas, Kate, Mrs Nickleby, and Smike to establish a more peaceful home beyond Ralph's direct control.

The Cheerybles ask Nicholas to assist Madeline Bray and her invalid father, who are trapped by debt but reluctant to accept charity. Nicholas and Madeline fall in love, though neither feels free to declare it. Kate and the Cheerybles' nephew Frank also grow attached. Ralph, seeking new means to wound Nicholas, allies himself with Wackford Squeers and the elderly moneylender Arthur Gride. Gride controls Arthur Bray's debts and wants to marry Madeline, while Ralph expects to profit from the arrangement. Madeline feels compelled to sacrifice herself to save her father. Meanwhile Squeers attempts to recapture Smike, whose terror and fragile health make the renewed persecution especially dangerous. John Browdie helps Smike escape, but the attacks leave the household conscious that Ralph will use any vulnerable person as leverage against Nicholas.

Nicholas learns of the proposed marriage between Madeline and Gride and rushes to stop it. Arthur Bray dies before the ceremony, freeing Madeline from the bargain made for his sake, and Nicholas carries her from the scene. Gride's house is robbed, and documents connected to Madeline's rightful property disappear into a chain of concealment that Ralph tries to exploit. Smike's health worsens, and Nicholas takes him into the country in hope of recovery. Smike confesses his love for Kate but asks nothing from her; after years of deprivation and fear, he dies with Nicholas beside him. Nicholas returns grieving but determined to secure Madeline's safety. Ralph continues working with Squeers and others against him, unaware that Newman Noggs is collecting evidence and that an old associate named Brooker knows a secret capable of destroying him.

Newman Noggs brings Ralph's enemies and victims together, and the missing documents establishing Madeline's inheritance are recovered. Brooker then reveals that Smike was Ralph's own son, hidden from him after Ralph rejected the boy's mother. Ralph learns that the nephew he persecuted had cared for his abandoned child, while his own plots helped drive Smike through terror and illness to death. Unable to bear the discovery and the collapse of his schemes, Ralph hangs himself. Squeers's crimes lead to transportation, and the boys at Dotheboys Hall rise against the school and disperse. Nicholas marries Madeline, whose property is restored, and Kate marries Frank Cheeryble. With the Cheeryble brothers' continuing friendship, the couples, Mrs Nickleby, and Newman Noggs return to the family's old country home. Nicholas and Madeline raise children there and keep Smike's memory alive, replacing the isolation and greed represented by Ralph with a durable household built on loyalty.

characters.description: An Englishman from York who rejects the secure life his parents planned and repeatedly goes to sea. Restless, practical, and intensely self-reliant, he narrates how disaster forces him to build a life with almost no human assistance.
characters.name: Robinson Crusoe

characters.description: Crusoe's elderly father, a prosperous immigrant who urges his youngest son to remain in England and enjoy a moderate, stable life. He warns that misery often follows those who abandon that middle condition.
characters.name: Crusoe's father

characters.description: A boy enslaved alongside Crusoe in North Africa. He helps Crusoe escape by boat and proves brave and capable during their voyage down the African coast.
characters.name: Xury

characters.description: The captain of a Portuguese ship that rescues Crusoe and Xury off the African coast. Generous and commercially shrewd, he helps Crusoe reach Brazil and begin life there as a planter.
characters.name: The Portuguese captain

characters.description: A man Crusoe rescues from captors on the island. Crusoe names him for the day of the rescue. Intelligent, energetic, and eager to learn, he becomes Crusoe's companion after decades of solitude.
characters.name: Friday

characters.description: Friday's father, brought to the island as a captive. His reunion with Friday gives Crusoe new information about nearby peoples and the fate of other Europeans.
characters.name: Friday's father

characters.description: A European survivor living among people on the mainland before Crusoe and Friday help rescue him. He becomes part of their plan to contact possible allies and enlarge the island settlement.
characters.name: The Spaniard

characters.description: The lawful commander of an English vessel seized by mutineers. Put ashore with loyal companions, he allies with Crusoe in an attempt to recover his ship.
characters.name: The English captain

characters.description: One of the most dangerous members of the mutinous English crew. Defiant and difficult to subdue, he is left on the island when the lawful captain regains control.
characters.name: Will Atkins

characters.description: A trusted friend in England who manages Crusoe's money after his early voyages. Her honesty helps preserve what remains of his affairs during his long disappearance.
characters.name: The widow

characters.description: Crusoe's business associate in Brazil, entrusted with part of the plantation when Crusoe leaves on a trading voyage. His management becomes important when Crusoe returns after many missing years.
characters.name: Crusoe's Brazilian partner

recaps.ending: Crusoe and Friday help an English captain defeat mutineers and recover his ship, giving Crusoe a route home after twenty-eight years on the island. Back in Europe, Crusoe learns that his Brazilian plantation has prospered and made him wealthy. He rewards those who acted honestly for him and provides for old friends. Avoiding another sea journey, he travels overland from Spain and survives attacks by wolves and a bear. He settles in England, marries, and has children. After his wife's death, his restlessness returns. He revisits the island, finds a troubled colony made up of the men left there and later arrivals, supplies it, and continues traveling before closing with the prospect of further adventures.
recaps.in_short: Robinson Crusoe defies his father's advice and goes to sea, enduring storms, enslavement, escape, and a new career as a Brazilian planter. A slave-trading voyage ends in shipwreck, leaving him alone on an island. He salvages tools and supplies, builds fortified homes, grows crops, raises goats, and slowly transforms terror and despair into a disciplined religious and practical life. After many years he finds evidence that groups visit the island to kill captives. He eventually rescues one captive, names him Friday, and teaches him English and Christianity. Together they save Friday's father and a Spaniard. When English mutineers land, Crusoe helps their captain recover his ship. After twenty-eight years he returns to Europe, discovers his plantation has made him rich, and later revisits the island settlement before resuming his travels.

recaps.text: Robinson Crusoe ignores his father's warning against a wandering life and secretly goes to sea. Early storms frighten him but do not cure his restlessness. On a later voyage he is captured by North African pirates and enslaved. After two years he escapes in a small boat with the boy Xury. A Portuguese captain rescues them and takes Crusoe to Brazil, where Crusoe establishes a plantation. Wanting labor and greater profit, he joins a voyage to the African coast. The ship is wrecked in a storm, and Crusoe alone reaches an uninhabited island.

Crusoe repeatedly swims to the wreck and salvages guns, powder, food, tools, timber, sails, and other supplies before the sea destroys it. He builds a fortified shelter backed by a cave, keeps a calendar, and begins a journal. Isolation first produces fear and despair, then a severe illness leads him to pray and reconsider his life. He learns to make furniture and containers, explores the island, and discovers that grain spilled from his supplies will grow. Through experimentation he plants crops and begins turning survival into a sustainable routine.

Crusoe surveys the island, builds a second country shelter, and tries unsuccessfully to make a boat he can move to the water. He domesticates goats, improves his harvests, makes rough pottery and clothing, and gains control over the seasonal rhythms of his new home. Years pass with no human company. Then he discovers a single footprint in the sand. The sign overturns his sense of safety. He strengthens his defenses and later finds evidence that visitors come to the island for ritual killings and feasts, though he hesitates to attack people whose customs he condemns but does not fully understand.

After further years of watchfulness, Crusoe sees captives brought ashore. He intervenes when one prisoner escapes, killing pursuers and saving the fugitive. Crusoe names the man Friday and begins teaching him English, European habits, and Christianity. Friday proves loyal and capable, while his knowledge explains the mainland and the visiting groups. He tells Crusoe that Europeans live among his people. When another party arrives with captives, Crusoe and Friday attack and rescue two men: Friday's father and a Spaniard. They plan to bring the other Europeans to the island and build a community strong enough to leave safely.

Before the planned rescue can proceed, an English ship anchors offshore and mutineers land with their lawful captain and two loyal men as prisoners. Crusoe reveals himself to the captain and offers help in exchange for passage to England. Using the island's terrain, hidden weapons, and divisions among the mutineers, the allies capture the shore party and retake the ship. Some rebels are pardoned into service; the most dangerous are left on the island with supplies and instructions. Crusoe departs after twenty-eight years, taking Friday with him.

Crusoe returns to England and finds his parents dead. Accounts from Brazil show that his plantation has prospered, making him wealthy. He repays the Portuguese captain's kindness, rewards his honest partner and the widow who guarded his affairs, and arranges his property. Traveling overland from Spain to avoid the sea, Crusoe and Friday survive wolves and a bear in the mountains. Crusoe later marries and has children. After his wife dies he again travels abroad and revisits the island, where the men left behind and later newcomers have formed an uneasy colony. He supplies and organizes the settlement, then resumes his travels and leaves the continuation of his adventures for another account.

characters.description: A tall, physically awkward wife and mother who has organized her life around her husband and children. Ruth is painfully aware that she does not resemble the kind of woman her husband admires. When he leaves her for Mary Fisher and dismisses her as a she-devil, she begins to treat that insult as permission to discard her old duties and remake her circumstances.
characters.name: Ruth Patchett

characters.description: Ruth's husband, an accountant whose comfortable suburban life depends heavily on her domestic work. Bobbo is vain, conventional, and impatient with Ruth, and he is conducting an affair with the successful novelist Mary Fisher.
characters.name: Bobbo Patchett

characters.description: A wealthy writer of romantic fiction who lives in a picturesque seaside tower. Mary has fashioned a graceful public life around beauty, love, and literary success, but her affair with Bobbo brings Ruth and the untidy demands of his family into that carefully controlled world.
characters.name: Mary Fisher

characters.description: Ruth and Bobbo's daughter. Nicola is one of the two children whose everyday care has fallen chiefly to Ruth and whose needs become much harder for Bobbo to ignore after he leaves the family home.
characters.name: Nicola Patchett

characters.description: Ruth and Bobbo's son. Like his sister Nicola, Andy is accustomed to his mother's constant care and becomes part of the practical burden that follows Bobbo into his new life.
characters.name: Andy Patchett

characters.description: Mary Fisher's elderly mother, who lives in an institution and has a difficult relationship with her daughter. She is less impressed by Mary's romantic self-image than Mary's admirers are, and her dependence makes the arrangements for her care a source of pressure.
characters.name: Mrs Fisher

characters.description: Mary Fisher's capable household servant at the tower. Garcia helps preserve the orderly, secluded life Mary has built and must absorb the domestic complications created by Bobbo's arrival.
characters.name: Garcia

characters.description: The judge assigned to Bobbo's criminal case. His authority over the proceedings makes his private weaknesses and susceptibility to influence consequential to Ruth's campaign.
characters.name: Judge Bissop

recaps.ending: Ruth completes the long physical reconstruction through which she has made herself resemble Mary Fisher's ideal of feminine beauty. Mary, meanwhile, loses the secure romantic world she had tried to preserve and dies. Bobbo serves his prison sentence for the financial crimes Ruth arranged to place around him. When he is released, he returns to the seaside tower, where Ruth now occupies Mary's former position. Their original marriage has not been restored: Ruth controls the money, the home, and the terms of their life together, while Bobbo is expected to please and serve her. Ruth has obtained the outward form and social power that once belonged to her rival, but the result is deliberately unsettling. Her liberation has become inseparable from manipulation, punishment, and the adoption of the very standards of beauty and dominance that once excluded her.
recaps.in_short: Ruth Patchett's husband Bobbo leaves her and their children for Mary Fisher, a beautiful and wealthy romance novelist. Taking his contemptuous description of her as a she-devil as a new identity, Ruth destroys the domestic role that confined her and pursues a methodical revenge. She transfers the burdens of children and family care to Bobbo and Mary, builds an employment business that gives her money and a network of women, and engineers records that make Bobbo appear responsible for financial crimes. He is convicted and imprisoned. Ruth then submits to an extended series of painful operations to transform her body toward Mary's appearance, while Mary's health, household, and fantasy of perfect love collapse. After Mary dies and Bobbo completes his sentence, Ruth occupies Mary's tower and takes Bobbo back on reversed terms: she holds the wealth and authority, and he becomes the dependent partner. Ruth wins the life she targeted, though her victory reproduces the same unequal power she set out to escape.

recaps.text: Ruth Patchett manages a suburban home, raises Nicola and Andy, and endures the open dissatisfaction of her husband, Bobbo. He is having an affair with Mary Fisher, a successful writer whose beauty, wealth, and seaside tower embody everything Ruth believes she lacks. Bobbo eventually announces that he is leaving his family for Mary and characterizes Ruth as a she-devil. Rather than plead for his return, Ruth accepts the hostile label and decides that the obedient wife he abandoned will cease to exist. She destroys the family home and makes sure that Bobbo must take responsibility for the children. What begins as marital rejection becomes a deliberate campaign: Ruth intends to dismantle the arrangements that protect Bobbo and Mary while freeing herself from the unpaid domestic role that has defined her.

With the Patchett home gone, Bobbo's new relationship can no longer remain a secluded romance. Nicola and Andy bring noise, work, and dependency into Mary's tower, straining the elegant life she has cultivated. Ruth refuses to resume her old duties. Moving through low-paid care and service work, she studies how institutions and households depend on women whose labor is easily ignored. She also turns her attention to Mary's elderly mother, another obligation Mary has kept at a distance. By shifting care responsibilities toward Mary, Ruth attacks not only the affair but Mary's preferred identity as a woman set apart from ordinary domestic demands. Ruth's apparent disappearance from her former life is therefore strategic: she is gathering experience and discovering how to convert other women's discontent into practical power.

Ruth establishes an employment enterprise that places women in domestic and office jobs. The business gives vulnerable workers an income while giving Ruth access to organizations, records, and people who would once have ignored her. She adopts new presentations of herself as circumstances require and accumulates money rather than remaining financially dependent on Bobbo. At the tower, Mary finds that love does not insulate her from children, an aging parent, servants, or Bobbo's selfishness. Ruth uses her expanding network to interfere with the financial world Bobbo understands best. Transactions and documents are arranged so that irregularities point toward him, turning his professional confidence into a liability. Her revenge is no longer an impulsive response to abandonment; it has become an organized project supported by the skills and alliances she acquired after leaving home.

The financial trail Ruth has constructed closes around Bobbo, and his insistence that he is innocent cannot overcome the records associated with him. Ruth also reaches into the legal process surrounding his prosecution, ensuring that the institutions he trusted do not rescue him. He is convicted and sent to prison, separating him from Mary and destroying the prosperous future for which he left his family. Ruth now possesses substantial financial and organizational power, but she does not stop after securing independence. She begins an extreme physical transformation, submitting to repeated surgery and bodily alteration so that she can acquire the proportions and appearance celebrated in women such as Mary. The process exposes the severity of Ruth's goal: she means to control both the social system that judged her and the image of femininity by which it judged her.

Ruth completes the painful sequence of operations that remakes her appearance in the image of the kind of woman Bobbo desired. Mary cannot preserve the tower as a sanctuary of perfect romance: Bobbo's imprisonment, family obligations, and her failing health strip away that fantasy, and she dies. Bobbo eventually finishes his sentence with his former confidence and independence broken. Ruth takes possession of the position Mary once occupied, including the tower and the material security surrounding it, and receives Bobbo back into her life. Their roles are now reversed. Ruth controls the household, wealth, and sexual terms of the relationship, while Bobbo is the dependent partner expected to accommodate her wishes. Her plan succeeds, but the conclusion does not present a simple recovery of self. Ruth has escaped subordination by mastering coercion, money, and conventional beauty, then uses those powers to create a new unequal arrangement with herself at its center.

characters.description: A boy of North African parentage who narrates his life in Belleville with a mixture of innocence, observation, and deliberately improvised logic. Known as Momo, he has been raised by Madame Rosa among the children of sex workers and is fiercely attached to her despite his fear that she will die.
characters.name: Momo

characters.description: An elderly Jewish woman, former sex worker, and survivor of Auschwitz who cares for other sex workers' children in her cramped sixth-floor apartment. Her health is failing, and memories of wartime persecution shape both her fears and the hidden refuge she keeps in the cellar.
characters.name: Madame Rosa

characters.description: An elderly Muslim carpet seller whom Momo visits for conversation. Monsieur Hamil is losing his sight and sometimes his memory, but he offers the boy affection, stories, and a religious perspective on love and endurance.
characters.name: Monsieur Hamil

characters.description: A compassionate physician who attends Madame Rosa and knows that her age and declining health limit what medicine can do. Momo turns to him for explanations while also resisting any plan that would separate Rosa from home.
characters.name: Doctor Katz

characters.description: A warm, imposing transgender woman from Senegal who once boxed and now works as a prostitute. Lola brings money, food, practical help, and reassurance to Madame Rosa's household, becoming one of Momo's most dependable adult friends.
characters.name: Madame Lola

characters.description: A Nigerian man whose business and personal difficulties are expressed in ceremonious visits to Madame Rosa's apartment. His presence connects the household to Belleville's wider immigrant community.
characters.name: N'Da Amédée

characters.description: A film editor whom Momo meets after following her in the street. Nadine responds to his loneliness with patience rather than alarm and allows him to see the unusual work of assembling film scenes.
characters.name: Nadine

characters.description: Nadine's husband, a man whose professional experience with children helps him meet Momo without treating the boy's guarded behavior as simply a problem.
characters.name: Ramon

characters.description: A distressed and mentally fragile man who arrives claiming to be Momo's father. He presses Madame Rosa for information about the child he left in her care years earlier.
characters.name: Youssef Kadir

recaps.ending: Madame Rosa's physical and mental decline reaches the point at which others want her hospitalized, something she has long feared. Momo instead helps her descend to the cellar room she prepared as a refuge from persecution. She dies there with him beside her. Unable to accept the separation and determined to protect her from institutions even after death, Momo stays with her body, disguising the odor with perfume and cosmetics while telling people she has gone away. The truth is discovered only after neighbors notice the smell. Momo is finally removed from the cellar and taken into the care of Nadine and Ramon, who have offered him a home. His devotion has not saved Rosa's life, but it has allowed him to honor her wish not to end it in a hospital and makes clear that love, rather than legal or biological ties, formed their family.
recaps.in_short: Momo, a Muslim boy of North African descent, lives in Belleville with Madame Rosa, an elderly Jewish survivor of Auschwitz who cares for the children of prostitutes. As Rosa's body and memory fail, Momo seeks help from neighbors including Monsieur Hamil, Doctor Katz, and Madame Lola, while fearing officials will take Rosa to a hospital. He learns that she has concealed both his real age and the violent history of his parents. He also meets Nadine and Ramon, who offer the possibility of another home. When Rosa can no longer climb or care for herself, Momo takes her to the cellar refuge she prepared against another persecution. She dies there, and he remains beside her body for weeks, concealing her death until the smell brings discovery. Momo then goes to live with Nadine and Ramon, carrying forward the lesson that his bond with Rosa was a family created by care rather than blood.

recaps.text: Momo lives in a sixth-floor Belleville apartment run by Madame Rosa, a former prostitute who is paid to raise the children of women still working in the trade. He does not know his exact age or much about his parents. Rosa is Jewish and survived Auschwitz; Momo is Muslim, and she has tried to preserve his religion while raising him. The apartment is crowded, poor, and held together by irregular payments and help from neighbors. Momo notices Rosa's worsening breathlessness, pain, and confusion and begins to fear losing the only parent he knows. He seeks companionship with Monsieur Hamil, an elderly Muslim carpet seller, and asks difficult questions about whether a person can live without being loved.

Madame Rosa's declining health makes the stairs and daily care of the children increasingly difficult. Doctor Katz can offer limited treatment, but Momo distrusts medical and welfare authorities because hospitalization would take Rosa away. Madame Lola, a transgender Senegalese woman and former boxer, becomes a generous source of food, money, and practical support. Momo wanders Belleville, invents stories, and sometimes acts out to make himself visible to adults, but repeatedly returns to protect Rosa. He also learns about the cellar room where she sometimes retreats. Stocked with a chair, candles, and reminders of her faith, it is her private shelter against the terror that another roundup might come.

As Rosa's memory becomes less reliable, Momo shoulders more of the household's burdens and watches the community rally around her. Monsieur Hamil's own failing memory shows Momo another version of old age. During his walks, Momo follows a woman named Nadine and eventually meets her. She is a film editor and treats him kindly, allowing him to visit and observe her work. Nadine and her husband Ramon begin to offer a connection outside the apartment, though Momo remains emotionally bound to Rosa and wary of being claimed or examined. His search for origins matters less to him than the immediate question of how to keep Rosa from being removed against her will.

A man named Youssef Kadir arrives and identifies himself as Momo's father. His appearance forces Madame Rosa to reveal that Momo is older than he has been told and that his mother was a prostitute whom Kadir killed during a mental breakdown. Rosa has hidden the boy's age in order to keep him with her longer. She protects Momo during the confrontation by confusing his identity with that of another child, and the shock of the encounter proves fatal to Kadir. The disclosures leave Momo with a clearer but painful account of his birth family. They also confirm that Rosa's deceptions, however damaging, arose from possessive love and fear of losing him.

Rosa deteriorates rapidly, drifting between the present and memories of persecution. Officials and neighbors recognize that she needs institutional care, but she has made Momo understand that she does not want to die in a hospital or be kept alive without awareness. Momo helps her down to the cellar refuge, telling others that she has left. He remains with her as she dies and continues sitting beside the body, applying perfume and makeup in an effort to preserve both her dignity and the fiction that they are still together. After weeks, the odor leads others to discover them. Momo is taken from the cellar and goes to Nadine and Ramon, whose family can give him a home. Rosa is gone, but Momo's final act expresses the loyalty between two people whose different religions, ages, and origins never prevented them from becoming family.

characters.description: A middle-school teacher trying to preserve ordinary routines as the natural and technological systems around him fail. Marty is separated from his wife Felicia but still turns to her when the scale of the ending becomes impossible to face alone.
characters.name: Marty Anderson

characters.description: Marty Anderson's former wife, who shares his alarm at the world's accelerating collapse. Their old intimacy survives the end of their marriage and gives both of them someone with whom to witness events they cannot prevent.
characters.name: Felicia Gordon

characters.description: An apparently ordinary accountant whose face suddenly appears on billboards and television messages thanking him for thirty-nine years. Marty and Felicia do not know him, yet the unexplained celebration of his life spreads as their world comes apart.
characters.name: Charles Krantz

characters.description: A young woman passing through Boston after an unsuccessful job interview. Janice stops when a street drummer's rhythm and Chuck's unexpected dancing turn a discouraging day into a spontaneous public performance.
characters.name: Janice Halliday

characters.description: A boy performing percussion on the streets of Boston. Jared's improvised beat draws Chuck out of the crowd and supplies the music for a dance that briefly brings strangers together.
characters.name: Jared Franck

characters.description: Chuck's grandmother and an enthusiastic dancer. Sarah raises him after the loss of his parents, fills the Krantz home with music and teaches him the steps that become one of his deepest private joys.
characters.name: Sarah Krantz

characters.description: Chuck's grandfather, an accountant who takes the orphaned boy into his home with Sarah. Albie encourages a practical career and firmly forbids Chuck from entering the locked cupola at the top of the house, a room he treats with genuine fear.
characters.name: Albie Krantz

recaps.ending: The final act in the book's reverse structure returns to Chuck's childhood. After his parents die, his grandparents Albie and Sarah raise him in a large house whose cupola is always locked. Sarah gives him a lasting love of dance, while Albie introduces him to accounting and warns him never to enter the room above. Chuck eventually learns why: the cupola can show a visitor a death that lies ahead. He enters and sees his own early death in a hospital at thirty-nine. The knowledge frightens him but does not stop him from choosing a full ordinary life, including work, love, family and the dance glimpsed in the preceding act. Chronologically, Chuck later dies from a brain tumor, and the immense inner world made from everyone and everything he has known ends with him. The book closes in his youth, with both his mortality and the multitudes of experience ahead of him held together.
recaps.in_short: The novella moves backward through Charles Krantz's thirty-nine years. First, teacher Marty Anderson and his former wife Felicia watch reality collapse while inexplicable advertisements thank an unknown accountant named Chuck. The destruction is the ending of the world contained within Chuck as he dies from a brain tumor. An earlier episode shows Chuck on a business trip in Boston, where a street drummer's rhythm prompts him to dance with stranger Janice Halliday, revealing a joy concealed by his conventional career. The final section follows his childhood after his parents' deaths. Raised by his grandparents Albie and Sarah, Chuck learns both accounting and dance. A forbidden cupola in their house can reveal a viewer's future death; Chuck enters and sees himself dying at thirty-nine. He nevertheless grows into the life already shown, embracing its work, family, music and fleeting connections despite knowing it will end.

recaps.text: Middle-school teacher Marty Anderson lives through an accelerating series of failures: communications disappear, disasters consume whole regions, and the physical world itself seems to be shutting down. Amid the collapse, advertisements appear everywhere thanking an unknown accountant, Charles Krantz, for thirty-nine years. Marty reconnects with his former wife Felicia, and the two face the approaching end together. The mystery resolves outside their awareness: Chuck is dying in a hospital from a brain tumor. The failing world belongs to his consciousness, assembled from the people, places and knowledge he has carried throughout his life. As Chuck dies at thirty-nine, that inner universe and everyone within it go dark.

The story moves backward to an ordinary day in Chuck's earlier life. In Boston on an accounting trip, he hears the inventive rhythm of a boy named Jared Franck, who is drumming on the street. Chuck unexpectedly begins to dance. Janice Halliday, disappointed after a job interview, joins him, and their skill and pleasure gather a crowd. The performance reveals an expressive side of Chuck that his business clothes and career do not announce. When the music ends, the strangers separate and continue with their lives, but the encounter becomes one of the countless moments contained within the man whose death was shown in the opening act.

The last section moves back to Chuck's childhood. After his parents die, he is raised by his grandparents Albie and Sarah Krantz. Sarah teaches him to dance and makes music a source of freedom; Albie, an accountant, encourages the stable profession Chuck will eventually choose. One part of their home remains forbidden: a locked cupola that Albie fears. Chuck discovers that the room can show a visitor a death from the future. When he finally enters, he sees himself dying in a hospital at only thirty-nine. The vision gives him knowledge of his limit, not a way to escape it. He proceeds toward the life the earlier acts have displayed: an outwardly conventional career, deep reserves of dance and music, connections to strangers, and an inner world vast enough to hold everyone he has known. The narrative ends with the young Chuck's future still before him, while the reader knows both its richness and its end.

characters.description: A failed wizard of Ankh-Morpork's Unseen University, expelled after one of the eight great spells of the Octavo lodged itself in his mind and crowded out everything he tried to learn afterwards. He can cast nothing, speaks several languages, and treats running away as a skill worth being good at. Since being pressed into service as guide to the Disc's first tourist he has been carried from one disaster to the next, and the book opens with him falling off the edge of the world. His hat is embroidered with the word wizzard.
characters.name: Rincewind

characters.description: A small, cheerful insurance clerk from the wealthy Agatean Empire on the far side of the Disc, and the first tourist the Discworld has ever had. He carries a picture-making box, a phrasebook, and an unshakeable belief that the world is fundamentally a friendly place put on for his benefit. He does not recognise danger when it is directly in front of him, which has so far worked out better for him than it has for anyone travelling with him.
characters.name: Twoflower

characters.description: Twoflower's travelling chest, made of sapient pearwood and moving on hundreds of small legs. It holds far more than its size allows, follows its owner across continents and through impossible places, and destroys anything that threatens him. It cannot be reasoned with, outrun, or left behind.
characters.name: The Luggage

characters.description: The vast star turtle on whose shell four elephants stand carrying the Discworld. Astronomers on the Disc have noticed that it has changed course and is swimming steadily toward a red star that grows larger in the sky with every passing day, and nobody knows why.
characters.name: Great A'Tuin

characters.description: The anthropomorphic personification of death, a robed skeleton with a scythe who speaks in a voice that arrives directly inside the listener's head. He collects the souls of the notable and the interesting, keeps a careful diary of appointments, and has been trying to keep an appointment with Rincewind for some time without success. He is patient, literal-minded, and increasingly curious about the living.
characters.name: Death

characters.description: The Archchancellor of Unseen University and the most senior wizard on the Disc, weighed down with ceremonial titles and a robe to match. Elderly, imperious, and thoroughly conventional, he treats magic as a matter of ritual and precedence. When the Octavo begins acting on its own he takes charge of the University's response and attempts to recover the missing spell by force of high magic.
characters.name: Galder Weatherwax

characters.description: A young senior wizard of Unseen University, unusual among his colleagues for being neither fat nor obviously magical. He keeps files, draws up organisational charts, and thinks of the University as an institution to be managed rather than a brotherhood of spellcasters. He is patient, tidy, and quietly determined to climb every rung of the eight orders of wizardry, and he pays close attention to what the Octavo is doing.
characters.name: Ymper Trymon

characters.description: A mercenary captain hired to bring Rincewind back to Unseen University alive. Competent, practical, and impatient with the men she leads, she is a professional in a trade that mostly attracts amateurs, and she pursues her quarry across country with more persistence than her employers expected.
characters.name: Herrena the Henna-Haired Harridan

characters.description: The Disc's greatest hero, now eighty-seven years old, toothless, thin as a stick, and still alive after a career that has killed every rival he ever had. He has been robbing temples and fighting monsters since before most kingdoms existed, owns almost nothing, and has strong opinions about the modern habit of wearing trousers. Age has cost him his teeth and much of his hearing but none of his speed or nerve.
characters.name: Cohen the Barbarian

characters.description: A young woman of the Circle Sea country who was chosen by her people's druids as a sacrifice at a stone circle, and who is unimpressed by the honour. Sensible, blunt, and quick to organise the people around her, she attaches herself to the travellers after being freed and takes a particular interest in Cohen.
characters.name: Bethan

characters.description: The keeper of Unseen University's library, the largest collection of magical books on the Disc. A surge of raw magic turns him into an orangutan, and once he discovers how convenient long arms are for reaching high shelves he declines every offer to be turned back. He communicates in a single syllable, is enormously strong, and is fiercely protective of the books in his care.
characters.name: The Librarian

characters.description: The Discworld's most powerful book of magic, written by the Creator and holding the eight great spells that underpin the world. It sits chained in a cellar beneath Unseen University, is aware of its own contents, and has begun taking an interest in the fact that one of its spells is missing.
characters.name: The Octavo

recaps.ending: Trymon takes the Octavo, reads seven of the eight great spells directly into his mind, and is immediately hollowed out and worn by the Things from the Dungeon Dimensions, which use him as a doorway into the world. Rincewind climbs the Tower of Art and confronts him, and after being pursued through a landscape inside Trymon's head he destroys him with a half-brick in a sock. With the Things beaten back, Rincewind reads the Octavo, the eighth spell finally leaving his mind, and the eight spells together settle the world. The red star turns out not to be a threat at all: Great A'Tuin was swimming to it to give birth, and eight small turtles hatch and swim away from the star carrying eight tiny worlds of their own, with the Disc passing safely by. Rincewind, at last free of the spell, can begin learning ordinary magic and returns to Unseen University as a student. Twoflower decides he has seen enough of the world and goes home to the Agatean Empire, leaving the Luggage behind as a parting gift to Rincewind, who is now stuck with it. Cohen the Barbarian and Bethan are married, and Cohen settles into a comfortable position in the Circle Sea kingdoms.
recaps.in_short: Rincewind and Twoflower fall off the edge of the Discworld and are saved when the great spell lodged in Rincewind's head rewrites reality to put them back on it, because it has work for him. A red star is growing in the Disc's sky and Great A'Tuin is swimming straight at it; the wizards of Unseen University learn that the eight spells of the Octavo must be read together to save the world, and one of them is inside Rincewind. Hunted by mercenaries hired by the ambitious wizard Trymon, the pair cross the continent with the aging hero Cohen the Barbarian and a rescued sacrifice named Bethan, while Trymon murders the Archchancellor and seizes control of the University. In Ankh-Morpork, with the star filling the sky and the city in the grip of panic and star cults, Trymon reads the Octavo himself and is possessed by creatures from the Dungeon Dimensions. Rincewind kills him at the top of the Tower of Art and reads the spells, and the star proves to be where Great A'Tuin was going to hatch eight baby turtles. Freed of his spell at last, Rincewind returns to the University, and Twoflower goes home, leaving him the Luggage.

recaps.text: Previously: Rincewind, an inept wizard expelled from Unseen University after one of the eight great spells of the Octavo lodged itself in his mind, was ordered by the Patrician of Ankh-Morpork to act as guide to Twoflower, the Discworld's first tourist, a rich and relentlessly optimistic insurance clerk from the distant Agatean Empire. Twoflower's introduction of insurance burned much of Ankh-Morpork to the ground, and the two fled the city together, accompanied by Twoflower's Luggage, a walking chest of sapient pearwood that is devoted to its owner and lethal to everyone else. Their travels took them through a temple of the ancient evil Bel-Shamharoth and the dragon-haunted Wyrmberg to the kingdom of Krull at the very Rim of the world, where scholars intended to sacrifice them to a voyage over the edge. They escaped, only to be swept over the Rimfall themselves, and the story broke off with the pair falling off the edge of the Discworld into open space.

As Rincewind and Twoflower fall off the Disc, reality shifts around them and they find themselves alive in a forest, deposited back on the world. The cause is the spell in Rincewind's head, one of the eight great spells of the Octavo, which has decided it needs him alive. At Unseen University the Octavo, the Creator's own book of magic, has begun acting without being asked; the wizards discover that the world is in danger and that all eight spells must be spoken together to save it. Above the Disc a red star has appeared and is growing, and Great A'Tuin, the turtle carrying the world, is swimming directly toward it. The Archchancellor, Galder Weatherwax, sets out to recover the missing spell by summoning Rincewind back to the University, watched closely by Ymper Trymon, an ambitious young wizard with a filing system and plans of his own. Death, meanwhile, continues to turn up wherever Rincewind is, and continues to be disappointed.

Galder's summoning fails to fetch Rincewind, so the University's response becomes less refined: a band of mercenaries under Herrena the Henna-Haired Harridan is hired to bring the wizard in alive. Rincewind and Twoflower keep moving through the countryside with Herrena's people behind them, at one point taking shelter in a shop that appears in places where no shop was and vanishes again afterwards, its owner condemned to wander between worlds. Across the Disc the red star grows brighter and ordinary people begin to notice it, and the wizards' assurances that everything is under control convince nobody. Panic follows: mobs form in the cities, wizards are blamed for whatever the star turns out to be, and cults spring up devoted to welcoming it.

Still pursued, Rincewind and Twoflower fall in with Cohen the Barbarian, the Disc's greatest hero, now eighty-seven, toothless and entirely undiminished in every other respect. Together they interrupt a druid ceremony at a stone circle, where a young woman named Bethan has been selected as a sacrifice, and get her away from the priests. Bethan joins the party and quickly makes herself indispensable, and she and Cohen take a clear liking to each other. At Unseen University, Galder Weatherwax dies in a magical accident that Trymon arranges and then presents as a tragedy, which leaves Trymon in charge of the University and of the search for the eighth spell. The raw magic now loose in the world also turns the Librarian into an orangutan; discovering that this makes shelving considerably easier, he refuses to be changed back. The star continues to swell in the sky, and magic itself begins to behave unreliably as the world approaches it.

The travellers cross troll country, where the local inhabitants turn out to be slow and stupid in the heat and sharp-witted in the cold, and Cohen is fitted with a set of diamond teeth that solve the greatest inconvenience of his old age. Herrena's band is still on their trail, and the Luggage, separated from its owner and thoroughly bad-tempered about it, crosses the country after them, leaving a trail of people who wish they had not got in its way. With the star now dominating the sky, magic failing across the Disc and the countryside emptying as people head for the cities or for the cults, the party turns toward Ankh-Morpork, where the Octavo and the other seven great spells are kept.

Twoflower is brought close to death and spends the interval in Death's own domain, where he introduces Death and the other Horsemen to a card game they find considerably more absorbing than their duties, which delays them at an awkward moment. The party reaches Ankh-Morpork to find the city in chaos. The red star fills half the sky, ordinary magic barely works, and the streets belong to mobs hunting wizards and to star cults preaching that the light is a deliverance. At Unseen University, Trymon has consolidated his authority and made himself the man who will save the world. Rather than gather the eight orders of wizards to read the spells as tradition requires, he takes the Octavo for himself and reads seven of the great spells directly into his own head, intending to hold all of that power alone. It is more than a human mind can contain. The Things from the Dungeon Dimensions, formless creatures pressing at the edges of reality, take him over and begin using him as a way in, and the Tower of Art at the heart of the University becomes the point where they will break through.

Rincewind climbs the Tower of Art to face what is left of Trymon, is drawn into the nightmare landscape inside his head, and kills him with a half-brick in a sock, driving the Things back out of the world. He then reads the Octavo, and the eighth spell leaves his mind at last; the eight spells spoken together steady the world. The red star proves to be no danger: Great A'Tuin was making for it in order to give birth, and eight small turtles hatch there and swim away carrying eight tiny new worlds, while the Disc passes safely on. Free of the spell for the first time in his life, Rincewind returns to Unseen University to begin learning magic properly. Twoflower, satisfied with his holiday, goes home to the Agatean Empire and leaves the Luggage to Rincewind as a gift. Cohen and Bethan marry, and Cohen accepts a comfortable place among the kingdoms of the Circle Sea.

characters.description: A twelve-year-old boy who has been expelled from a string of schools for trouble he cannot explain, and who struggles with dyslexia and attention problems. Loyal to his mother and fiercely protective of his friends, he is quick-tempered and impulsive but brave. Strange and dangerous things keep happening around him, and he is about to learn why.
characters.name: Percy Jackson

characters.description: Percy's closest friend at Yancy Academy, a nervous boy with a limp and a medical excuse from physical activities who always seems to be watching out for Percy. Easily frightened and quick to make excuses, he is more than he appears and takes his role in Percy's life very seriously.
characters.name: Grover Underwood

characters.description: Percy's devoted mother, who works long hours at low-paying jobs and protects her son with warmth and humor despite an unhappy marriage. She loves the sea and takes Percy to a rented cabin at Montauk beach that holds special meaning for her. She has kept important truths about Percy's father from him to keep him safe.
characters.name: Sally Jackson

characters.description: Percy's crude, selfish stepfather, a heavy gambler who reeks of cigars and beer and treats Percy and Sally with open contempt. Percy privately calls him Smelly Gabe.
characters.name: Gabe Ugliano

characters.description: The immortal centaur who has trained heroes for thousands of years, hidden for a time as Percy's kindly, wheelchair-using Latin teacher Mr. Brunner. As the activities director of Camp Half-Blood, the safe haven for children of the Greek gods, he guides and instructs the young demigods with patience and quiet authority.
characters.name: Chiron

characters.description: The god of wine, sentenced by Zeus to run Camp Half-Blood as punishment and forbidden to drink wine while he serves out his term. Irritable, bored, and dismissive of the campers, he can barely be bothered to remember their names.
characters.name: Dionysus

characters.description: A sharp, strategic demigod with gray eyes and blond hair who has lived at Camp Half-Blood for years and longs to prove herself on a real quest. A daughter of Athena, she is a skilled fighter and planner who tends to Percy when he first arrives, sizing him up at once.
characters.name: Annabeth Chase

characters.description: The friendly, well-liked head counselor of the Hermes cabin, an older camper who welcomes Percy, teaches him swordsmanship, and treats newcomers kindly. He carries a scar across his face and speaks with some bitterness about feeling overlooked by the gods.
characters.name: Luke Castellan

characters.description: A tough, aggressive camper and daughter of Ares, the god of war, who bullies newcomers and takes an immediate dislike to Percy, shoving his head toward a toilet on his first day at camp.
characters.name: Clarisse La Rue

characters.description: The god of the sea and one of the three most powerful gods. During a game he publicly claims Percy as his son, an act that breaks a sworn pact among the greatest gods not to father more children and makes Percy's very existence a source of danger and suspicion. He is a distant father but not an unkind one.
characters.name: Poseidon

characters.description: The god of war, who meets the travelers on their journey in the guise of a swaggering, leather-clad biker. Aggressive and eager for conflict, he strikes a bargain with Percy, offering help and supplies in exchange for a favor.
characters.name: Ares

characters.description: The grim lord of the Underworld and god of the dead, brother of Zeus and Poseidon. Suspected of stealing Zeus's master lightning bolt to start a war among the gods, he is the target Percy's quest leads toward, and he receives Percy in his shadowy palace with fury and his own accusations.
characters.name: Hades

recaps.ending: Percy recovers Zeus's master bolt, defeats the god Ares in single combat using his powers over water, and returns the bolt to Mount Olympus, averting war among the gods; he also forces the return of Hades' stolen helm of darkness. Meeting his father Poseidon face to face, Percy is acknowledged, though the two remain distant. Back at Camp Half-Blood he learns that the entire theft was engineered to set the gods against one another, and that the real thief was Luke Castellan, the counselor who had befriended him, secretly serving the reviving Titan lord Kronos, who seeks to overthrow the gods. Luke tries to kill Percy with a venomous scorpion and then flees to continue serving Kronos. Percy's mother, released from the Underworld, frees herself from her cruel husband Gabe by turning him to stone with Medusa's severed head. Offered the chance to stay at camp year-round, Percy instead decides to live at home and attend school with his mother, keeping a foot in the mortal world. The threat of Kronos and Luke's betrayal remains open for the books to come.
recaps.in_short: Twelve-year-old Percy Jackson discovers that the Greek gods are real and that he is a demigod, the son of the sea god Poseidon. After a monster attack seems to kill his mother, he reaches Camp Half-Blood, a training ground for the gods' children. When Zeus's master lightning bolt is stolen, Percy is blamed, and to prevent a war among the gods he sets out with his friends Annabeth and Grover to find the true thief before the summer solstice. Their journey across the country toward the Underworld's entrance in Los Angeles pits them against monsters and gods, including Ares, who deceives them. In the Underworld Percy learns the bolt has been planted in his own bag and that his mother is held captive; he escapes but must leave her behind. He defeats Ares, returns the bolt to Mount Olympus, and stops the war. He then learns the real thief was his camp friend Luke, secretly serving the reviving Titan lord Kronos. Percy comes home to find his mother freed and chooses to spend the school year in the mortal world.

recaps.text: Twelve-year-old Percy Jackson keeps getting expelled from schools for bizarre incidents he cannot explain. On a class trip to a museum, one of his teachers transforms into a winged monster and attacks him, and afterward everyone insists she never existed and was never his teacher. His anxious friend Grover behaves strangely, and his Latin teacher, Mr. Brunner, seems to know more than he admits. At home Percy is caught between his loving mother, Sally, and his crude, unpleasant stepfather, Gabe. Sensing danger, Sally takes Percy to a seaside cabin, where Grover catches up to them and reveals that monsters are hunting Percy. A bull-headed creature attacks on the road; Percy's mother is seized and vanishes in a flash of gold, and Percy kills the monster before collapsing at the border of a mysterious camp.

Percy wakes at Camp Half-Blood, a hidden haven for the children of the Greek gods, who turn out to be real and still active in the modern world. Mr. Brunner is revealed to be Chiron, an immortal centaur, and the camp is overseen by the sour god Dionysus. Percy meets other young demigods, including the clever Annabeth, the friendly counselor Luke, and the hostile Clarisse, and learns that a camper's godly parent is often unknown. During a game of capture the flag, Percy's power over water surfaces and he is publicly claimed as a son of Poseidon, a forbidden birth under an oath among the most powerful gods. Chiron then reveals that Zeus's master lightning bolt has been stolen and Percy is being blamed; to head off a war among the gods, Percy accepts a quest to recover it, with suspicion pointing toward the Underworld far to the west.

Percy sets out west with Annabeth and Grover toward Los Angeles, where an entrance to the Underworld is said to lie. Vengeful monsters pursue them at every turn: the winged Furies attack aboard a bus, and at a roadside garden statuary shop they narrowly kill Medusa, whose gaze turns victims to stone. At the Gateway Arch in St. Louis, Percy is cornered by the fire-breathing Chimera and its mistress; badly hurt, he escapes by plunging into the Mississippi River, where he discovers he can breathe and heal underwater. The travelers press on, low on money and time, racing against a summer-solstice deadline before the gods go to war.

As they continue across the country, the travelers encounter the god Ares, who strikes a bargain with them: in exchange for aid he sends them to retrieve his shield, which leads them into a trap in an abandoned amusement park that they barely escape. They pass through the Lotus Hotel and Casino in Las Vegas, a place where time stands still and guests forget to leave, and only just break free after realizing that days have slipped by and their deadline is closing. Reaching Los Angeles at last, Percy outwits a monster running a waterbed store and finds the hidden entrance to the Underworld.

Percy, Annabeth, and Grover cross the river of the dead and reach the palace of Hades. There Percy discovers, to his horror, that the stolen master bolt has been hidden in his own backpack without his knowledge, and Hades furiously accuses him of also stealing his helm of darkness. Percy finds his captured mother held in the Underworld, but with only three magic escape pearls for four people, he is forced to leave her behind to save his friends and complete the quest. Escaping to a beach, the three are met by the god Ares, who is revealed to have set Percy up and arranged for the bolt to be planted on him. Percy defeats Ares in a duel with his sea powers, forcing him to return Hades' helm, and recovers the master bolt.

Percy flies to New York and climbs to Mount Olympus, returning the master lightning bolt to Zeus and averting war among the gods. He meets his father, Poseidon, who acknowledges him though the two remain distant. Back at Camp Half-Blood, Percy learns the deeper truth: the theft was meant to turn the gods against each other, and the real thief was Luke, the friendly counselor, secretly working for the reviving Titan lord Kronos, who wants to destroy the gods. Luke tries to kill Percy with a venomous scorpion before escaping to serve Kronos. At home, Percy finds his mother alive and freed from her cruel husband Gabe, whom she has turned to stone with Medusa's head. Given the choice to live at camp year-round, Percy decides to spend the school year at home with his mother, knowing that greater dangers, and Kronos, still lie ahead.

characters.description: A Los Angeles criminal-defense lawyer who conducts much of his practice from the back seat of a Lincoln Town Car. Twice divorced and accustomed to representing clients he assumes are guilty, he prizes procedure, leverage, and the prosecution's burden of proof. A lucrative assault case interrupts his routine and tests the emotional distance on which his career depends.
characters.name: Mickey Haller

characters.description: Haller's driver, a former client working off part of his legal debt. He navigates the lawyer among Los Angeles courthouses and meetings, helping turn the Lincoln into a mobile office.
characters.name: Earl Briggs

characters.description: A bail bondsman who directs Louis Roulet's family toward Haller. His referral promises the kind of well-funded client the defense lawyer rarely sees and gives Haller an immediate financial reason to take the case.
characters.name: Fernando Valenzuela

characters.description: Haller's case manager and second ex-wife. Efficient and sharply familiar with his habits, she manages calls, schedules, and money from a distance while remaining part of the unconventional professional network surrounding him.
characters.name: Lorna Taylor

characters.description: A Los Angeles prosecutor, Haller's first ex-wife, and the mother of their daughter, Hayley. She objects to his willingness to exploit doubt for dangerous clients, but their family ties and lingering affection keep them in one another's lives.
characters.name: Maggie McPherson

characters.description: Mickey and Maggie's young daughter. Haller's limited time with her is one of the clearest measures of what his work and divorces have cost, and concern for her makes threats against his family especially powerful.
characters.name: Hayley Haller

characters.description: A wealthy Beverly Hills real-estate agent accused of beating and attempting to rape a woman he met in a bar. Polished, indignant, and supported by his mother, he insists he was lured into a setup and offers Haller a rare client able to finance a full defense.
characters.name: Louis Roulet

characters.description: Roulet's mother, a wealthy businesswoman protective of her son and prepared to pay for an aggressive defense. Her influence and money stand behind Roulet's insistence that the charge is an attempt to exploit him.
characters.name: Mary Windsor

characters.description: The lawyer who represents the Roulet family and helps retain Haller for Louis's criminal case. Formal and watchful, he protects the family's interests while leaving trial strategy to the defense specialist.
characters.name: Cecil Dobbs

characters.description: The woman whose report leads to Roulet's arrest. A bar hostess and sex worker, she says Roulet followed her home, struck her, and threatened her with a knife before she was able to raise an alarm.
characters.name: Regina Campo

characters.description: Haller's regular private investigator and a former police officer. He checks witnesses, physical evidence, and Roulet's background, giving Haller an independent account of a case whose surface facts appear unusually favorable to the defense.
characters.name: Raul Levin

characters.description: A former client serving a life sentence for the murder of Martha Renteria. Haller persuaded him to accept a plea rather than risk execution, but Menendez has always maintained that he did not kill her.
characters.name: Jesus Menendez

characters.description: The deputy district attorney assigned to prosecute Roulet. Young and ambitious, he treats the case as a direct contest with Haller and relies on the victim's account, forensic evidence, and jailhouse information to withstand the defense attack.
characters.name: Ted Minton

recaps.ending: Haller obtains Roulet's release on the current assault charge by exposing weaknesses and manipulation in the prosecution's case, even though he has become convinced Roulet attacked Regina Campo and murdered Martha Renteria.
